## What is in this section

Three documents, in ascending order of length:

1. **The one-page team note** — for a team of two to fifteen who need a
   rule by Friday.
2. **The firm policy** — for a practice with clients, engagement terms
   and a regulator.
3. **The client-facing paragraph** — the wording you put in an engagement
   letter or a proposal when a client asks how you use these tools.

Take whichever fits, put your own name in the brackets, delete what does
not apply, and have someone who carries risk read it before you circulate
it. All three are starting drafts and general information, not legal
advice. Rules differ by jurisdiction and profession and they change.

There is also a free web version of the one-page note that assembles it
from nine questions. It is on the same site this pack came from, under
Free tools. It runs entirely in your browser and collects nothing.

---

## 1. The one-page team note

> **USING AI TOOLS — [TEAM OR FIRM NAME]**
>
> **Applies to:** everyone in the team, including contractors.
> **Owner:** [name and role]. **Next review:** [date].
>
> **Why this exists.** We use these tools because they save real time.
> They also produce confident, well-written output that is sometimes
> wrong. This note exists so the time saved is not paid back later with
> interest, and so nobody has to guess what is allowed.
>
> **Approved tools.** [List them.] Anything not on this list is not
> approved yet — that is not a refusal, ask and the list can grow.
> Personal accounts and free consumer tiers are not approved for any work
> involving client material.
>
> **What may go in.** [Choose one: no client or personal data at all /
> client data only in the approved tools whose terms state our input is
> not used for training / anonymised material only.] Identification
> numbers, bank details and payroll figures for named individuals stay
> out regardless of the tool. If you are unsure whether something counts,
> it counts. Ask first.
>
> **What you check before it goes out.** Every figure, every quotation,
> every reference, every claim about a rule — against its source.
> Recalculate anything numerical independently. Never cite a standard, a
> case or a section you have not opened yourself.
>
> **What we tell clients.** [Choose one: internal aid, not routinely
> disclosed / we answer honestly and specifically when asked / we state
> it in engagement terms.] We never deny using these tools.
>
> **Where they are not to be used.** Signing, approving or certifying
> anything. Any final decision about a person's pay, employment or
> standing. Anything under privilege, live dispute or investigation
> without written approval. Anything you would not be able to check.
>
> **Records.** Where a tool materially helped produce a deliverable, note
> it in the working papers: which tool, what for, who checked it. One
> line is enough.
>
> **If something goes wrong.** Tell [owner] the same day. Say plainly
> what happened. Nobody is disciplined for reporting quickly. Concealment
> is the only thing treated seriously.

## 2. The firm policy

Longer, for a practice that has clients and a regulator. The clauses
below are drafting blocks — keep the ones that apply.

### 2.1 Purpose and scope

This policy governs the use of artificial intelligence tools in the work
of [FIRM]. It applies to all partners, employees, contractors and
temporary staff, on any device, whether the tool is provided by the firm
or not. It covers general-purpose assistants, AI features embedded in
software the firm already licenses, transcription and note-taking tools,
and any tool that sends firm or client material to a third party for
processing.

It does not change any existing duty. Where this policy and a
professional obligation appear to conflict, the professional obligation
governs and you raise it with [ROLE] immediately.

### 2.2 Responsibility

The person who signs, reviews or issues a piece of work is fully
responsible for it. That responsibility is not reduced, shared or
transferred by the use of any tool. "The system produced it" is not an
explanation the firm will offer to a client, a regulator or a court, and
it is not one you may offer internally.

### 2.3 Approved tools and how the list changes

Only tools on the approved register may be used for client work. The
register is maintained by [ROLE] and records, for each tool: the
provider, the licence tier, whether firm input may be used to train the
provider's models, where data is processed, the retention period, and the
date the terms were last reviewed.

Requesting an addition is normal and encouraged. Using an unapproved tool
on client material is a disciplinary matter, not because the tool is
suspect but because the firm cannot answer for what it cannot see.

### 2.4 Client and personal information

[Choose the stance that matches the firm's risk appetite and delete the
others.]

*Option A — prohibition.* No client information, personal data or
confidential material may be entered into any AI tool. This includes
names, initials, entity names, account numbers, identification numbers,
addresses and figures attributable to a named person or client, and it
includes combinations of details that would identify someone together
even if each is innocuous alone.

*Option B — approved tools only.* Client information may be entered only
into tools on the approved register whose terms state that firm input is
not used to train the provider's models and is not retained beyond the
period recorded on the register. It may never be entered into a personal
account or a consumer tier.

*Option C — anonymised only.* Only material from which identifying
details have been removed may be entered. Where anonymising would take
longer than performing the task unaided, perform the task unaided.

In every case: identification numbers, bank account details, payroll
figures for named individuals, health information and anything received
under an explicit confidentiality undertaking stay out.

### 2.5 Verification

Before AI-assisted work leaves the person who produced it:

(a) every figure is recalculated or agreed to source;
(b) every quotation, reference, standard and authority is opened and
    read in the original;
(c) the reasoning is read as though a reviewer were trying to break it,
    with particular attention to anything stated confidently and without
    qualification;
(d) [for higher-risk work] a second qualified person reviews the
    deliverable and records that they have done so.

Fluent output is not verified output. These tools are at their most
persuasive on the things they have invented.

### 2.6 Disclosure

[Choose one.] The firm does not deny the use of these tools in any
circumstances. Where a client asks, the answer given is honest and
specific: what the tool was used for, what it was not used for, and who
checked the result.

### 2.7 Prohibited uses

AI tools are not to be used to: sign, certify, approve or give an opinion;
make a final decision about any individual's employment, remuneration,
credit or professional standing; process any matter under legal
privilege, live dispute or regulatory investigation without the written
approval of [ROLE] for that specific matter; produce anything the user
would be unable to verify; or generate material presented as the
independent work of a person who did not review it.

### 2.8 Records

Where an AI tool materially contributed to a deliverable, the working
papers record the tool, the purpose, and the reviewer. This is not
bureaucracy. It is what allows the firm to answer a question about the
work two years after the engagement closed.

### 2.9 Incidents

Any suspected error in issued work, or any client material entered
somewhere it should not have been, is reported to [ROLE] on the day it is
noticed. Prompt reporting attracts no sanction. Concealment does.

### 2.10 Review

This policy is reviewed every [3/6/12] months by [ROLE], and sooner if a
tool on the register materially changes its terms, if the firm's
professional body or regulator issues guidance, or if an incident
suggests a clause is not working. Superseded versions are retained.

## 3. The client-facing paragraph

For engagement letters and proposals. Short on purpose — clients want to
know you have thought about it, not to read your internal policy.

> **Use of technology.** We use software tools, including tools that use
> artificial intelligence, as an aid in performing our work. They are
> used under a written internal policy which restricts what information
> may be processed, requires that outputs be verified against source
> before use, and prohibits their use for judgements and approvals. The
> individuals named in this engagement remain fully responsible for the
> work and for every conclusion in it. We are happy to describe our
> approach in more detail on request.

If your engagement terms already contain a confidentiality or
subcontracting clause, check that this paragraph sits consistently with
it rather than beside it.

---

## Before you adopt any of this

These are drafts assembled from general practice, not legal advice, and
not a statement of compliance with any law, standard or professional
requirement. Requirements differ between jurisdictions and professions
and they change. Have whoever carries risk in your organisation read the
version you intend to use, and check it against your regulator's current
guidance and your own client engagement terms.
